tip.title: Purpose, tone, and word choice
tip.text: Beyond persuade, inform, entertain, skilled writers have precise purposes: to warn, to honor, to mock, to comfort. TONE is the writer's attitude, carried by WORD CHOICE. "The official declined to comment" is neutral; "the official dodged the question" is critical. To read tone, find the loaded words and ask what they make you feel. Irony is when the words say one thing and mean the opposite; a sarcastic compliment is still a criticism.

passage.title: In Praise of the Waiting Shed
passage.text:
Let us take a moment to honor the waiting shed on the national highway outside our town, that monument to civic planning.

Built in 2019 at a cost, according to the plaque, of 1.2 million pesos, the shed offers travelers a roof, three benches, and a view of the exact spot where the jeepneys do not stop. The jeepneys stop fifty meters down the road, at the corner by the bakery, where they have stopped since before anyone can remember. Commuters therefore have a choice: sit in the shade and miss their ride, or stand in the sun and catch it. Most choose the sun. The benches, polished by rain and nothing else, remain in excellent condition.

The plaque bears the names of four officials, in letters larger than the word "shed." It does not bear the name of whoever decided where the shed should go, which is a pity, because that person deserves recognition.

I am told that a second shed is planned for the other side of the highway. I hope it, too, will be built with the same care, and that the commuters there, like us, will learn to admire it from a distance.

words.meaning: a structure built to honor something; also used mockingly for something that shows a failure
words.example: The empty mall is a monument to bad planning.

words.meaning: relating to a town or city and its people
public credit or praise for something done
words.example: She received recognition for her bravery.

items.prompt: What is the author's REAL purpose?
choices: To sincerely praise the waiting shed
To criticize wasteful, poorly planned public projects through irony
To inform readers where the jeepneys stop
To ask for a third shed
items.why: Every "praise" is undercut by facts showing the shed is useless; the piece mocks the project.

items.prompt: Which sentence BEST supports the idea that the shed cost a lot for what it delivers?
choices: "Let us take a moment to honor the waiting shed."
"Most choose the sun."
"Built in 2019 at a cost... of 1.2 million pesos, the shed offers travelers a roof, three benches, and a view of the exact spot where the jeepneys do not stop."
"I am told that a second shed is planned."
items.why: The sentence puts the price beside the result: 1.2 million pesos for a roof, three benches, and a view of nothing useful.

items.prompt: How does the waiting shed COMPARE with the corner by the bakery?
choices: The shed is older than the corner and has more benches.
The shed is new and costly but unused; the corner is old and unofficial but where jeepneys actually stop.
Both are places where jeepneys stop.
The corner was built by the four officials; the shed was not.
items.why: The shed was "built in 2019" for 1.2 million pesos, while jeepneys stop at the corner "where they have stopped since before anyone can remember."

items.prompt: According to the passage, what is the trade-off between sitting in the shed and standing in the sun?
choices: The shed is cooler but farther from the bakery; the sun is hotter but closer to it.
The shed is free; standing in the sun costs money.
In the shed you get shade but miss your ride; in the sun you get burned but catch it.
Both choices let commuters catch the jeepney; the shed is just more comfortable.
items.why: Commuters can "sit in the shade and miss their ride, or stand in the sun and catch it." Each choice gains one thing and loses another.

items.prompt: "The benches, polished by rain and nothing else, remain in excellent condition." What is the author really saying?
choices: The benches are well made.
No one ever uses the benches.
It rains often in the town.
The benches should be cleaned.
items.why: "Polished by rain and nothing else" means no person has ever sat on them. The compliment is ironic.

items.prompt: Which sentence BEST supports the claim that commuters do not use the shed?
choices: "Most choose the sun."
"The plaque bears the names of four officials."
"The shed offers travelers a roof."
"A second shed is planned for the other side of the highway."
items.why: Given the choice between shade and catching the jeepney, "most choose the sun," meaning they stand away from the shed.

items.prompt: Which word choice MOST signals the ironic tone in the first sentence?
choices: "national highway"
"monument to civic planning"
"outside our town"
"take a moment"
items.why: Calling a shed a monument is deliberately grand; readers soon learn it is a monument to bad planning.

items.prompt: "That person deserves recognition." What does the author actually mean?
choices: The planner should get an award.
The planner should be held responsible for a foolish decision.
The planner's name was forgotten by accident.
The officials were generous.
items.why: The author wants the person who chose the useless location to be named, not honored.

items.prompt: Which FACT in the passage most strongly supports the author's criticism?
choices: The shed has three benches.
The jeepneys stop fifty meters away at the corner where they have always stopped.
The plaque has four names.
A second shed is planned.
items.why: The shed was built where the jeepneys do not stop; this single fact makes the project pointless.

items.prompt: How does the author expect the planned SECOND shed to compare with the first?
choices: It will be built in a better spot where jeepneys stop.
It will be just like the first: built with the same "care" and admired by commuters from a distance.
It will be cheaper and have more benches.
It will be worse because it is on the other side of the highway.
items.why: The author hopes it "will be built with the same care" and that commuters "like us, will learn to admire it from a distance," meaning equally useless.
